To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
older Canadians are less likely to meet the guideline for physical activity if they have a chronic disease and the most common type of physical activity reported is walking.
older adults who have one or more chronic disease are less likely to be physically active than those without a chronic disease.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the health benefits of physical activity in the older Canadian population, and how chronic disease impacts physical activity levels.
the health of the elderly, particularly with the effects of aging on physical and psychological functioning.
understanding the determinants of leisure-time physical activity in older Canadians.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
physical activity is important to healthy aging.
older Canadians are less active than they should be and that the risk of not being active is even greater for people with chronic diseases.
older adults with chronic disease are less active than their peers who are disease-free and that this is an important health concern that needs to be addressed.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the majority of older adults do not meet recommended levels of physical activity, and that chronic disease is a risk factor for low physical activity levels.
physical activity should be promoted to all adults, but in particular those who are older and have a chronic disease, to improve their overall health and well-being.
older Canadians with chronic diseases are less physically active and this needs to be addressed by the healthcare system.
The main takeaway from our work is that
older adults need to be more physically active and that chronic disease does not preclude physical activity.
older adults with chronic diseases need to be more physically active to improve their health.
we need to do more as a society to promote physical activity in older adults.
